title: Scalars and Vectors

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 11 — Motion in a Plane

summary: A scalar has only magnitude; a vector has both magnitude and direction, and vectors must be combined using vector algebra, not ordinary addition.
explanation: A scalar quantity (mass, distance, speed, temperature, energy, time) is completely described by a number and a unit. A vector quantity (displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum) needs a magnitude AND a direction to be fully specified. Because direction matters, vectors add by the triangle/parallelogram law rather than plain arithmetic: two vectors of magnitude 3 and 4 units can give a resultant anywhere from 1 to 7 depending on the angle between them (resultant R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cosθ)). A unit vector (magnitude 1, written with a cap, e.g. î, ĵ, k̂) specifies pure direction along the x, y, z axes, so any vector A can be written as A = Axî + Ayĵ + Azk̂. Vector subtraction is addition of the negative vector (−B reverses B's direction), and the dot product (scalar result, A·B = AB cosθ) versus cross product (vector result, |A×B| = AB sinθ, direction by the right-hand rule) are the two ways vectors combine to give physically meaningful scalar or vector outputs — work is a dot product, torque is a cross product.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming two vectors always add like plain numbers (e.g. 3 + 4 = 7) — this is only true when they point in exactly the same direction; the angle between them changes the resultant.
Treating negative sign on a scalar-looking component as meaning 'negative magnitude' — for a vector it just means the component points opposite to the chosen positive axis.
Confusing the dot product (gives a scalar, used for work) with the cross product (gives a vector, used for torque and angular momentum).
examples: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N acting at right angles combine to a resultant of 5 N (3-4-5 triangle), not 7 N.
Displacement of 5 m east is a vector; distance travelled of 5 m has no direction attached and is a scalar.
genZNote: Magnitude alone isn't enough — vectors need a whole GPS pin, not just a number.
